guide.title: Electromagnetic induction: review guide
guide.intro: A changing magnetic flux creates an emf. This unit applies Faraday's and Lenz's laws to coils and moving rods, then studies inductors, which resist changes in current.
guide.equationNote: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. In exponential growth and decay, e ≈ 2.718 (so e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37).

sections.title: Faraday's law
body: Magnetic flux through a loop is Φ_B = ∫B·dA, or BA cos θ for a uniform field. Faraday's law: the induced emf is ε = −N dΦ_B/dt for a coil of N turns.
The flux can change because the field changes, the area changes, or the loop rotates. A rod of length L sliding at speed v through a perpendicular field has a motional emf ε = BLv.
points: Differentiate the flux, not the field alone, when the area also changes.
A constant flux, however large, induces nothing.
Keeping a rod moving at constant speed takes a force equal to the magnetic drag on it, ILB.

sections.title: Lenz's law
body: Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself.
This is energy conservation at work. The induced current always makes forces that resist the motion causing it, as with eddy currents that slow a magnet falling through a metal tube.
points: Increasing flux into the page: the induced field points out of the page, from a counterclockwise current.
Decreasing flux: the induced field points the same way as the original, to prop it up.
Eddy currents in solid conductors turn kinetic energy into thermal energy.

sections.title: Inductance and LR circuits
body: An inductor opposes changes in its current: ε = −L dI/dt. It stores energy U = ½LI² in its magnetic field.

When a battery is connected to an inductor and resistor in series, the current rises as I = (ε/R)(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with time constant τ = L/R. When the battery is removed, the current decays as I₀e^(−t/τ).
points: Just after switching on, the inductor acts like a break in the circuit (I = 0); long after, like a plain wire.
After one time constant, the rising current has reached about 63% of its final value.
An inductor's emf depends on how fast the current changes, not on the current itself.

example.prompt: A 0.30 H inductor and a 15 Ω resistor are connected to a 6.0 V battery at t = 0. Find the time constant, the final current, and the current at t = 0.020 s.
example.solution: τ = L/R = 0.30/15 = 0.020 s, and the final current is ε/R = 0.40 A. At t = τ, I = 0.40(1 − e⁻¹) ≈ 0.25 A.

misconceptions: “A strong magnetic field induces a current.”
Only a changing flux induces an emf.
“The induced field always opposes the original field.”
It opposes the change: if the flux is shrinking, the induced field points the same way as the original.
Long after switching on, an ideal inductor acts like a plain wire.
“The current in an LR circuit jumps to ε/R at once.”
It rises gradually, with time constant L/R.

questions.prompt: A 100-turn coil of area 0.010 m² sits in a perpendicular magnetic field that drops steadily from 0.50 T to 0.10 T in 0.20 s. What is the size of the average induced emf?
choiceExplanations: 0.40 is NAΔB, without dividing by the time.
0.020 V is the emf of a single turn; all 100 turns add.
200 V leaves out the coil's area.

questions.prompt: A single loop of area 0.050 m² lies perpendicular to a magnetic field B(t) = 0.20t³ tesla (t in seconds). What is the size of the induced emf at t = 2.0 s?
choiceExplanations: 0.080 is the flux at t = 2.0 s, in webers; the emf depends on its rate of change.
0.24 V differentiates 0.20t³ as 0.60t³ without lowering the power.
0.040 is Φ/t, an average rate from t = 0, not the rate at t = 2.0 s.

questions.prompt: A metal rod 0.50 m long slides along two rails at a constant 3.0 m/s through a perpendicular 0.40 T magnetic field. The rails are joined by a 0.20 Ω resistor (the rod and rails have no resistance). What force must be applied to keep the rod moving at constant speed?
questions.explanation: ε = BLv = (0.40)(0.50)(3.0) = 0.60 V, so I = ε/R = 3.0 A. The magnetic force on the rod opposes its motion with size ILB = (3.0)(0.50)(0.40) = 0.60 N, so an equal applied force keeps the speed constant.
choiceExplanations: Constant speed means zero net force, not zero applied force: the applied force must balance the magnetic drag.
1.8 is the power in watts (Fv = I²R = 1.8 W), not the force.
3.0 is the current in amperes, not the force.

questions.prompt: A magnetic field pointing into the page through a wire loop is increasing. Which way does the induced current flow, as seen from the front?
choices: It depends on the loop's resistance
questions.explanation: The flux into the page is increasing, so the induced current makes a field out of the page to oppose the increase. By the right-hand rule, a counterclockwise current makes a field out of the page inside the loop.
choiceExplanations: A changing flux always induces an emf, and a closed loop carries a current.
Resistance affects the size of the current, not its direction.
A clockwise current makes a field into the page, which would add to the increase instead of opposing it.

questions.prompt: A strong magnet dropped through a vertical copper pipe falls much more slowly than it does outside the pipe. Copper isn't magnetic. Why does the magnet slow down?
choices: Its moving field induces currents in the pipe whose fields oppose its motion
Air trapped in the pipe slows it down
The pipe's friction against the magnet slows it down
Copper attracts magnets, like iron does
questions.explanation: As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring of the pipe changes, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law their magnetic fields oppose the change, pushing back on the magnet; the lost kinetic energy becomes heat in the pipe.
choiceExplanations: The effect happens even with plenty of room for air to escape, and it vanishes in a pipe made of an insulator.
The magnet can fall without touching the pipe's walls and still slow down.
Copper isn't attracted to magnets; the effect needs the magnet to be moving.

questions.prompt: The current in a 0.50 H inductor is increasing at 4.0 A/s. What is the size of the emf across the inductor?
choiceExplanations: 8.0 divides the rate by L.
0.13 divides L by the rate instead of multiplying.
The emf is zero only when the current is steady; here it is changing.

questions.prompt: A 0.40 H inductor and a 20 Ω resistor are connected in series to a 12 V battery. What are the circuit's time constant and its final current?
questions.explanation: τ = L/R = 0.40/20 = 0.020 s. Long after switching on, the inductor acts like a plain wire, so I = ε/R = 12/20 = 0.60 A.
choiceExplanations: 8.0 multiplies L and R; the time constant is L/R.
240 multiplies ε by R; Ohm's law gives I = ε/R.
50 is R/L, the ratio upside down.

questions.prompt: In the circuit with τ = 0.020 s and a final current of 0.60 A, what is the current at t = 0.020 s after the battery is connected?
choiceExplanations: 0.22 A is 0.60e⁻¹, which describes a decaying current, not a rising one.
0.60 A is reached only long after switching on, not after one time constant.
0.30 A is half the final current; one time constant gives about 63%, not 50%.

questions.prompt: How much energy is stored in a 0.40 H inductor carrying 0.60 A?
choiceExplanations: 0.12 is ½LI; the current must be squared.
0.14 J leaves out the factor ½.
0.24 is LI, not an energy.
